name: Red velvet cake
origin: A Southern American butter cake distinguished from devil's food by a much smaller dose of cocoa (traditionally reacting with buttermilk and vinegar to a faintly reddish-brown crumb, well before commercial red food colouring became standard) and a cream-cheese frosting rather than chocolate icing.

ingredients.note: many red velvet formulas use oil rather than butter for an especially moist, tender crumb; see catalog.ts module notes on the missing vegetable-oil substance record
cocoa fraction of a small 5%-of-flour cocoa dose, far below devil's food's — red velvet is a lightly-cocoa'd butter cake, not a chocolate cake; split as in devils-food.json

classic recipes add a little vinegar for the bicarbonate to react against, alongside buttermilk's own acidity; vinegar's mass is a few percent of flour, folded into the liquid figure above rather than tracked as its own line

process.name: cream fat and sugar
process.description: beat oil (or softened butter) and sugar together

process.name: add eggs and cocoa
process.description: beat in eggs, then the small dose of sifted cocoa powder

process.name: alternate flour and buttermilk
process.description: fold in flour (with bicarbonate and salt) and buttermilk in alternating additions

notes: Structurally a lightly-cocoa'd American high-ratio butter cake (Gisslen's high-ratio method again), distinguished from devils-food.json mainly by a far smaller cocoa dose (5% of flour vs 20%). The cream-cheese frosting that defines red velvet visually and by taste is a separately-prepared component applied after baking, out of scope for this batter's formulation (see catalog.ts scope note); food colouring is omitted as a negligible, non-physically-meaningful mass.
